extraction_limitations: The uploaded PDF is an accepted manuscript; publication date beyond year 2026 was not reported in the supplied file.
The paper references Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Figures, but those supplementary materials were not included in the uploaded PDF and were not atomized.

Background claims that primarily summarize cited prior literature were not exhaustively atomized; extraction prioritized study-specific design, results, author interpretations, limitations, and provenance.
Some tabular percentages in the parsed PDF appear layout-sensitive; atoms preferentially use narrative values or unambiguous table cells and avoid internally inconsistent parsed percentages.

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to describe changes in the epidemiology of NDM-producing CRE compared with KPC-producing CRE from 2018 through 2023 across 10 U.S. population-based surveillance sites.
The surveillance network comprised 10 Emerging Infections Program sites covering 43 counties/areas, with an estimated 2023 surveillance population of 23,176,096 persons.

population.label: Residents of 10 EIP CRE surveillance areas

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: During 2018-2023, the surveillance system identified 8,421 incident CRE cases among 7,226 patients.

population.label: Patients with incident CRE cases in 10 EIP sites, 2018-2023

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: An incident CRE case was the first isolation within a 30-day period of E. coli, Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes, K. oxytoca, K. pneumoniae, or K. variicola resistant to any carbapenem from urine or a normally sterile site in a surveillance-area resident.

population.label: Surveillance-area residents with qualifying CRE isolate
inclusion_criteria: Specified Enterobacterales species resistant to doripenem, ertapenem, imipenem, or meropenem

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Colonization screening cultures were excluded from the CRE surveillance case definition.

population.label: CRE surveillance case ascertainment

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Cases were classified as healthcare-associated when hospital-onset or when community-onset with specified prior healthcare exposures; cases without those documented healthcare risk factors were classified as community-associated.
Any positive carbapenemase test result from a clinical laboratory, state public health laboratory, or CDC was sufficient to classify a CRE case as carbapenemase-producing CRE.

CDC characterization of submitted isolates included MALDI-TOF species identification, reference broth microdilution with an integrated metallo-beta-lactamase screen, modified carbapenem inactivation testing, and real-time PCR for blaKPC, blaNDM, blaVIM, blaIMP, and blaOXA-48-like genes.

Whole-genome sequencing was performed on submitted 2018-2022 CRE isolates that were CDC-confirmed carbapenem resistant and carbapenemase-gene PCR-positive or mCIM-positive; 2023 sequence data were unavailable for this analysis.
Annual crude incidence rates were calculated with surveillance case counts and U.S. Census population estimates, and temporal trends were tested with the two-tailed Mann-Kendall test.

Comparative analyses were restricted to cases positive only for NDM or only for KPC; categorical variables were compared with chi-square or Fisher exact tests and continuous variables with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.
The multivariable logistic regression model compared NDM-CRE with KPC-CRE and included year, epidemiologic classification, sex, age group, and organism as prespecified covariates.
Statistical significance was defined as P<0.05.
CDC reviewed the surveillance activity and deemed it not research; EIP sites likewise deemed it non-research or granted IRB approval with waiver of informed consent.
Of 8,421 incident CRE cases, 7,044 (83.6%) were tested for carbapenemase production.

population.label: Incident CRE cases in 10 EIP sites, 2018-2023

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Among 7,044 CRE cases tested for carbapenemase production, 1,707 (24.2%) were classified as CP-CRE.

population.label: Carbapenemase-tested incident CRE cases

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Among 1,707 CP-CRE cases, 1,002 (58.7%) were KPC-CRE and 364 (21.3%) were NDM-CRE.

population.label: CP-CRE cases

quantitative_result.effect_measure: proportion of CP-CRE that were KPC (%)

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Among 1,707 CP-CRE cases, 131 (7.7%) were OXA-48-like, 13 (0.8%) were IMP, 8 (0.5%) were VIM, and 140 (8.2%) had an unknown carbapenemase gene because molecular testing was not performed.

population.label: CP-CRE cases

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Forty-nine CP-CRE cases had more than one carbapenemase gene detected, and 37 of those 49 (75.5%) included blaNDM.

population.label: CP-CRE cases with multiple carbapenemase genes

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Overall crude CRE incidence increased from 5.34 per 100,000 population in 2018 to 7.65 per 100,000 in 2023, with a significant increasing trend (P=0.02).

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: No significant incidence trends were observed for NDM-producing Enterobacter spp. or Klebsiella spp.

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Among KPC-CRE isolates, the number of unique sequence types stayed relatively constant or decreased over time; ST131 predominated among KPC-E. coli and ST258 among KPC-K. pneumoniae from 2018 through 2022.

Among NDM-CRE isolates, greater sequence-type diversity was detected as more isolates became available; ST405 and ST167 were the most frequently identified NDM-E. coli sequence types, while ST147 and ST16 were the most common among NDM-K. pneumoniae.
The authors concluded that the rise in overall CRE incidence from 2018 to 2023 coincided with and was likely driven in important part by the sharp increase in NDM-CRE incidence.
The authors interpreted the higher frequency of community association and younger age among NDM-CRE cases as evidence of an emerging epidemiologic pattern distinct from KPC-CRE.
Because about 40% of community-associated NDM-CRE cases with available travel data did not report international travel, the authors considered local community transmission of NDM-CRE possible.
The authors interpreted the greater sequence-type diversity among NDM-CRE relative to KPC-CRE as consistent with efficient horizontal spread of NDM-conferring genes across different strains.

The authors recommended continued surveillance and additional work to identify risk factors for community-associated NDM-CRE, including patient interviews about community and outpatient healthcare exposures.
The 10-site EIP surveillance area may not be representative of the entire U.S. population, limiting generalizability.
Respiratory cultures and non-intraoperative wound cultures were excluded because infection and colonization are difficult to distinguish, which may have led to underestimation of CRE incidence.

Not all CRE isolates underwent carbapenemase testing or gene typing, and some external laboratory results may not have been captured, so CP-CRE incidence may be underestimated and some KPC- or NDM-CRE cases may have been misclassified.
Carbapenemase testing coverage ranged from 73% to 89% annually, was at least 84% from 2019 onward, and was 84% overall during the analysis period.

population.label: Incident CRE cases in 10 EIP sites, 2018-2023

validated_atoms.canonical_statement: Healthcare exposures documented outside the available medical record may have been missed, potentially causing nondifferential misclassification of epidemiologic class.
Travel history had substantial missingness and therefore was not included in the multivariable model.
The surveillance data could not determine when or where CRE acquisition occurred, including whether acquisition was local after international travel.
Only a subset of isolates underwent whole-genome sequencing and 2023 sequence data were unavailable, so observed allele and sequence-type distributions may not represent all cases.
Sequence data are available in NCBI under BioProject PRJNA288601.
The work was supported by CDC through the Emerging Infections Program cooperative agreement CDC-RFA-CK17-1701, with additional support from the CDC Genomic Sequencing Laboratory.
All authors reported no potential conflicts of interest.
